evidence.craft: Read src/rain_twin/model.py (107 lines), tests/test_model.py, experiments/run.py. Clean, small, stdlib-only, each function documented, sensible choice of bisection (strictly decreasing function) and Newton for Lambert W. Defects: var_atten is only valid for r a whole number of cells (docstring says so, no assertion); r_det lower bracket 1e-6 and hardcoded iters=50 (precision ~2e-14 km, fine) but no guard for r_fs<=0 or ell<=0; brier is O(fields x ranges) pure Python (fine at this size); the 'irreducible' Brier is computed in-sample from the same sorted sample used as the ensemble, noted as in-sample in the label; magic numbers in run.py but they mirror the paper. No dead code found.
evidence.claims: Checked each README/whitepaper number against experiments/results.txt: Jensen 1.52, 0.055 vs 0.084 dB/km, 18.84 km, 39%, median 18.56, 5th percentile 16.31, mean-matched 18.31 km and 59%, Brier 0.101/0.055/0.054/0.038/0.040/0.046, sd 0.81 to 2.27 km, 30% to 75%, ensemble 0.028-0.060 vs 0.043-0.104: all match. The stylisation caveat (k and gamma illustrative, not ITU calibrated, simulated truth, i.i.d. cells, single target) is stated in README and paper. Weak spots: the headline 'fixing the mean does not make a deterministic range right' and 'ensemble beats deterministic twins' are properties of a world generated by the ensemble's own model family, which the paper flags only as 'a single-parameter-set finding'; 'README title says what an ensemble fixes' is slightly stronger than evidence from an in-family simulation supports. No disclaimer beyond 'Stylised' (appropriate for a research page).
evidence.fitness: Nearest prior work: Jensen/mean-field bias for power-law rain attenuation is standard (rain-fade statistics in ITU-R P.530 and P.837/P.838 use rain-rate distributions, not mean rates; Crane's 'Electromagnetic Wave Propagation Through Rain' and the path-reduction-factor literature handle spatial rain structure; stochastic rain-cell and Monte Carlo fade simulators exist). The README cites only Skolnik and P.838 and names ARPG/RECUV as directions, not as prior art on rain-fade statistics, so novelty is not placed against that literature. The sound, reusable pieces are the exact Lambert-W uniform-rain range, the closed-form moment ratio and variance, and the twin-fidelity framing (score a twin by Brier against ensemble outcomes). The result itself (mean-rate model is biased; use a distribution) is an expected consequence of convexity, not new; the cell-length reversal (optimistic to pessimistic) is a mildly interesting but unvalidated observation, with the explanation only asserted ('median falls below mean for skewed sums'). A researcher could reuse the code as a teaching toy; they could not build on it as a rain model because nothing is fit to measured rain data.
evidence.domain: A propagation engineer would accept the physics (power-law specific attenuation, 40 log10 two-way radar-equation margin, Lambert-W for uniform rain) but would object that: rain is not i.i.d. exponential per 1 km cell with p=0.2 (real rain-rate distributions are lognormal-like with heavy tails and strong spatial correlation, and ITU path-reduction handles that); the detection model is a deterministic threshold with no SNR distribution, Swerling fluctuation or noise; there is no frequency, polarisation, beam-filling or wet-radome treatment; k, gamma are not tied to a band. The paper says so honestly, which lifts it above a 1, but it is a pedagogical sketch rather than a signed-off method.

defects.what: Closed-form var_atten is effectively untested: a seeded mutation (halving the (E R^g)^2 term) passes all 9 tests because the MC variance check has delta 0.12.
Headline Brier and range numbers have no regression test; run.py output is not compared to results.txt in any test or check.

Novelty is not placed against rain-fade statistics literature (ITU-R P.530/P.837 rain-rate distributions, path reduction factor, Crane); the Jensen gap on a convex power law is textbook and the ensemble-wins result is in-family by construction.
Cell-length explanation ('median attenuation falls below the mean for skewed sums') is asserted, not tested; var_atten silently assumes r is a whole number of cells.
Live page could not be loaded from the audit environment (proxy HTTP 000); unverified.

verdict: The arithmetic is right and the work reproduces: nine tests pass, run.py reproduces results.txt byte for byte, and my own independent code (plain bisection instead of Lambert W, different seed, 20000 fields) matched the Jensen ratio, both twin ranges, the real range quantiles, the reach probabilities and the clear-air and mean-rate Brier scores within Monte Carlo error, and every README number matches results.txt. It is small, honest about being stylised, and clean stdlib code. It does not meet the bar because verification is 2 (a seeded error in the variance formula passes the suite and no test pins the headline Brier results) and because the research value is modest: the result is a Jensen-inequality consequence in a simulated world drawn from the ensemble's own model family, with no fit to rain data and no placement against the established rain-fade statistics literature. A cheap fix would be a golden-file test of results.txt plus a tight check on var_atten, and a related-work paragraph citing ITU-R P.530/P.837 and Crane.
